newsitem.title: BOSNIA: "Secret" tunnel damages Sarajevo airport runway.
newsitem.headline: "Secret" tunnel damages Sarajevo airport runway.

text.p: Bosnian aviation authorities have closed one end of the main runway at Sarajevo airport because a "secret" wartime tunnel underneath it is collapsing, NATO said on Tuesday.

"The restriction is because the load-bearing capacity of the runway has been degraded by the gradual collapse, over a protracted period of time, of a tunnel constructed during the conflict," explained NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock.

"There is in excess of 2,000 metres (yards) of usable runway left which allows the airfield to remain open for military and the many types of civilian aircraft that currently use the airfield. It is only the last 600 metres that are closed."
Separatist Serb forces laid siege to the Bosnian capital of Sarajevo in the spring of 1992, a siege not fully lifted until the Dayton peace agreement was initialled a year ago this week.

From June 1992 Sarajevo's airport was controlled by U.N. forces and used to stage the world's longest lasting humanitarian airlift, which flew in food, clothing and medical supplies for about 380,000 people trapped in the city.

The airport marked an active front-line between government and Serb forces. Serbs held ground at both ends of the runway and Moslem forces controlled the neighbourhoods of Dobrinja and Butmir which flanked either side.

In order to move troops, arms, officials, civilians and supplies in and out of the besieged city, government authorities built a muddy, makeshift tunnel under the runway, connecting Dobrinja and Butmir.

Workers used hand tools to dig the tunnel as surreptitiously as possible while U.N. forces looked the other way as a matter of policy. The tunnel opened in 1993 and soon became the worst- kept secret in Bosnia.
Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic and other top officials were pulled through the tunnel seated on a bench mounted on a wheeled sled which ran over a narrow-gauge track.
Soldiers and civilians slogged the 800 metres (yards) stooped over in an awkward crouch.
Among the most ghastly scenes of the war was the torch-lit procession of soldiers' coffins and sheet-shrouded bodies hauled into Sarajevo for burial after battles outside the city.
A second, professionally engineered and constructed tunnel begun in 1995 has since been completed and is being maintained, presumably as a hedge against a resumption of war in Bosnia.
NATO officials said on Monday the second tunnel posed no threat to the operational integrity of the airport runway.
Haselock reported that Bosnian government authorities were mulling how and when to make the repairs which the original tunnel's progressive collapse make necessary.
